questions.prompt: Which branch in the tree is the highest-priority finding?
options: lsass.exe with a rundll32.exe child, since lsass never legitimately has children
questions.explanation: There is exactly one lsass.exe, parented by wininit.exe, with no legitimate children -- and the rundll32 involvement points directly at credential dumping in progress.

questions.prompt: Why is explorer.exe showing a non-running parent PID NOT a finding?
options: Explorer always runs without a parent
userinit.exe launches explorer.exe and then exits by design, leaving a normal orphan on every healthy Windows system
The parent PID field is unreliable in all cases
questions.explanation: Flagging this is the trap the drill is built around -- knowing what is normal prevents real findings being buried under false ones.

questions.prompt: What two independent violations does svchost.exe (PID 4820) exhibit?
options: Wrong path and wrong user context
Parented by powershell.exe rather than services.exe, and launched with no -k argument
Wrong session ID and missing signature
Too many child processes and high memory use
questions.explanation: services.exe is the only legitimate parent of svchost.exe, and every legitimate instance carries a -k argument naming its service group.

questions.prompt: What makes the winword.exe to powershell.exe branch compound rather than a single indicator?
options: It appears twice in the tree
The parent-child relationship is illegitimate on its own, and the -w hidden plus -enc flag cluster adds an independent signal
Word is running from a non-standard path
questions.explanation: Office has no legitimate reason to launch a script interpreter, and the hidden-window plus encoded-command combination is separately characteristic of malicious use.
